entries.title: Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgery to remove lump on lung
entries.summary: The pontiff said he would be operated on "in the coming days" to remove a lung nodule, which he said was found at "a very early stage."
entries.content:
Vatican

Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgery to remove lump on lung

October 11, 2026

The pontiff said he would be operated on "in the coming days" to remove a lung nodule, which he said was found at "a very early stage."

Pope Leo XIV said Sunday that he will undergo surgery this week to remove a lump on his lung.

"During recent medical checks, a nodule on my lung was found. It has been detected at a very early stage and is very localised," the 71-year-old said during his weekly address in St Peter's Square in the Vatican.

"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it. The operation is already planned in the coming days," he added.

What do we know about the pope's condition?

This is his first major health scare since the 71-year-old American became pope in 2025.

A lung nodule is a small, contained lesion that is smaller than 3 centimeters (1 inch) and can be benign.

According to the American Thoracic Society, fewer than 5% of lung nodules turn out to be cancerous.

The American Cancer Society says the nodules sometimes appear on CT scans of the chest or abdomen during searches for trauma or lung infections that are unrelated to cancer screenings.

Leo is younger than most popes. His predecessor, Francis, was five years older when he assumed the role, while Francis' predecessor, Benedict XVI, was 78 at the start of his tenure.

Leo is not known to have had any previous health issues, and leads a relatively active lifestyle.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: A migrant boat sank off the coast of Djibouti with the UN reporting over 200 people dead or missing
entries.summary: The UN migration agency has reported that at least 109 people were killed and 116 remain missing after a migrant boat sank overnight on its way to Yemen. At least 80 Ethiopians survived the incident but 15 children died.
entries.content:
October 11, 2026

The UN migration agency has reported that at least 109 people were killed and 116 remain missing after a migrant boat sank overnight on its way to Yemen. At least 80 Ethiopians survived the incident but 15 children died.

The United Nations International Organization for Migration (IOM) on Sunday said that 109 people were killed, 80 survived and 116 remained missing after the overnight sinking of a migrant boat off the coast of Djibouti in northeastern Africa.

The vessel, which was estimated to have been carrying 350 people, capsized near Obock, Djibouti, en route to Yemen.

In a statement, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac called the loss of life "devastating," adding, "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities" by trying to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and reach Gulf countries.

"Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East," according to the IOM.

IOM representatives said, "Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations as fears grow for those still missing."

Djibouti to Yemen a dangerous crossing

The IOM says it has detected more than 20,000 crossings from Djibouti to Yemen — which is currently in the middle of a raging civil war — in the past month. More than 900 migrants were killed attempting the passage in 2025.

The IOM says most of those attempting to cross are from Ethiopia and Somalia. The 80 survivors from Saturday night's capsizing were all Ethiopian nationals.

The IMO on Sunday urged "donors and partners to strengthen support for Djibouti's response, including search and rescue operations and life-saving assistance."

Of the bodies so far recovered, 52 were men, 42 were women and 15 were children.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Poland on alert amid possible attack on PM, defense minister
entries.summary: Poland was holding an emergency meeting after police received information about a possible assassination plot against PM Donald Tusk. The meeting comes amid a wave of violence at Polish schools this week.
entries.content:
Poland

Poland on alert amid possible attack on PM, defense minister

October 11, 2026

Poland was holding an emergency meeting after police received information about a possible assassination plot against PM Donald Tusk. The meeting comes amid a wave of violence at Polish schools this week.

Authorities in Poland were meeting on Sunday to discuss a potential assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defence ‌Minister ⁠Wladyslaw ⁠Kosiniak-Kamysz, Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Galecka said.

The emergency meeting at the Internal Security Agency's (ABW) Counter-Terrorism Center was convened after police received information about a possible attack, Galecka said in a post on X.

While the nature of the apparent threat was not immediately clear, the meeting comes as Polish authorities are on high alert after a wave of violent attacks at schools in the country this week.

Poland, which borders Ukraine, has also been facing growing security threats from hybrid attacks by Russia in recent months.

What do we know about the school attacks in Poland?

Poland is reeling from three knife attacks at schools in just four days this week, which have left at least one person dead and injured many others, including children.

The first incident was on Wednesday, when a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the central Mazovian province injured nine people when he attacked his fellow students and teachers with a sharp object.

A day later, a 15-year-old killed a school caretaker and injured two others at his former school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, also in the same province. Tusk said the suspect had worn a camera mounted to his helmet to film the attack.

On Saturday, a 21-year-old woman attacked an adult education school in Warsaw, wounding three other women.

Polish police have detained 117 people across the country for carrying knives or dangerous weapons, as well as for threatening to attack schools or students. Police checked 64,000 schools, most of them in central Mazovian province.

Police said Friday that cybercrime investigators have found no evidence that a social media challenge is fueling the wave of youth violence, or that the attacks were coordinated.

What did Tusk say about the attacks?

On Sunday morning, Donald Tusk said the attacks were "spontaneous actions" that were fueled by rising "glorification of violence" online.

"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said during the government crisis meeting.

"In the past years and months, we have noted — globally and in Poland — a rise in the fascination with violence," Tusk continued.

The prime minister blamed "nihilistic violence" for the wave of attacks, rather than a specific political ideology. However, he did acknowledge that "some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment."

Tusk added that authorities have observed an increase in online searches for Nazi or far-right content and for "mass killers who have become idols online."

The prime minister pointed to a "civilizational phenomenon" of children becoming more exposed to violence online through video games or crime stories.

Tusk added that police checks would continue at schools across the country next week to make sure children who have been exposed to these stories of knife attacks do not "get stupid and unsafe thoughts" of perpetrating copycat attacks.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Pakistan: President puts Khan stronghold province under emergency rule
entries.summary: President Asif Ali Zardari has effectively suspended the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The northwestern state is an epicenter of support for former PM Imran Khan and run by his PTI party.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan: Khan stronghold province put under emergency rule

October 11, 2026

President Asif Ali Zardari has effectively suspended the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The northwestern state is an epicenter of support for former PM Imran Khan and run by his PTI party.

Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari on Sunday announced that the northwestern Pakistani province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been put under emergency rule, effectively removing power from former Prime Minster Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.

The imposition of emergency rule comes as thousands of Khan supporters continue to stage anti-government protests and demand the former leader be released from jail.

Current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif proposed the move, which Zardari signed into order on Sunday.

The suspension of regional government was justified under constitutional articles that allow the central government to confront security threats and give it sweeping powers in emergency situations.

Sharif's government claims regional authorities have not done enough to curb Islamist violence in the province.

Why is Pakistan's government taking control of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa?

Last Sunday, thousands of Khan's supporters began to make their way from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad.

Organizers had declared their intent to rally hundreds of thousands more along the way in hopes of bringing about Khan's release from prison.

Despite being jailed since 2023, Khan, a popular former cricket star, maintains great influence in Pakistan, with he and his followers convinced that his imprisonment is the result of political persecution.

Khan, who began his term as prime minister in August 2018, was ousted from office in April 2022 after losing a no-confidence vote.

He has been in prison since August 2023.

Beyond corruption and treason charges, he was also accused of inciting violence after widespread anti-government protests in May 2023. Khan rejects the charges as a politically motivated plot to keep him away from power. He remains a popular political figure in Pakistan.

Khan's supporters claim that the 2024 election that brought Shehbaz Sharif back to power was rigged — an accusation the government denies.

Pakistan has seen a resurgence of terror attacks over the past several months and the Sharif government accuses Khan's PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, which is largely thought to be behind the attacks. 

The PTI rejects these accusations as a baseless smear campaign.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Yemen's Houthis warn passengers not to use Saudi airports
entries.summary: The warning from the Iran-backed rebels comes a day after a missile attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and injured more than 300. The airport will remain closed until at least Sunday night.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Yemen's Houthis warn passengers not to use Saudi airports

October 11, 2026

The warning from the Iran-backed rebels comes a day after a missile attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and injured more than 300. The airport will remain closed until at least Sunday night.

Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday warned passengers not to use airports in Saudi Arabia, a day after a deadly missile attack on Riyadh airport.

The attack, which killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300, is the deadliest on any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.

"The Yemeni armed forces renew their warning to all aviation and navigation companies, experts, staff, workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace," military spokesman Yahya Saree said on X.

"The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces," he said, adding that the airports of Mecca and Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam, would not be targeted.

The spokesman cautioned that the rebels' warning should be taken "seriously", and that Saudi Arabia "bore responsibility" for failing to intercept the missiles that struck the airport on Saturday.

Operations at Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, were suspended after Saturday's attack.

Air traffic monitor Flightradar24 said the airport's closure has been extended until at least 9 p.m. Sunday.

What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attack?

Although the Houthis have not formally claimed responsibility, Saudi officials have blamed the Iran-backed rebel group for Saturday's attack on the airport in the Saudi capital.

The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, has vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "fully-fledged war crime."

The missile strike on Riyadh comes amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure.

The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.

The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies, have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago.

While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humantiarian crisis.

How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes?

US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable."

Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels.

On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport.

The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation."

"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwaves sent through the world," von der Leyen said.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".

"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Germany sticks to Russia sanctions after Trump diesel deal
entries.summary: After Washington announced a sanctions pause on Russian diesel, Germany has said it remains committed to pressuring Moscow and supporting Ukraine. More on DW.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany sticks to Russia sanctions after Trump diesel deal

Published October 10, 2026last updated October 11, 2026

After Washington announced a sanctions pause on Russian diesel, Germany has said it remains committed to pressuring Moscow and supporting Ukraine. More on DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Merz's CDU gathers for leadership meeting addressing electoral free fall
  • The German government has said it will continue working with EU partners on Russia sanctions
  • Ex-Chancellor Schröder faces criticism for attending Putin's birthday
  • 'Ragebait' voted Germany's youth word of the year

Read below for a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, October 10, and Sunday, October 11.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Merz's CDU huddles to find way out of electoral free fall

Merz's CDU huddles to find way out of electoral free fall

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) will kick off a two-day leadership meeting on Sunday to plot a path out of the electoral crisis the party finds itself in after three dismal state elections.

The 25-member leadership meeting was called after the CDU — until now one of Germany's two largest popular parties — failed to even clear the 5% hurdle to enter Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's state legislature. The stinging loss, which Merz himself described as "a disaster," represented the first time in the party's history that it was booted from a statehouse. 

The CDU has been struggling to hold off the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party and has been thrust into an identity crisis due to the rate at which it is losing voters to the party.

In one of the summer's other elections — in Saxony-Anhalt — the CDU dropped nearly 20 percentage points, getting clobbered by the AfD, which racked up over 40% of the vote.

This weekend's meeting is designed to address voter dissatisfaction with the CDU-led governing coalition with the Social Democrats (SPD), as well as looking at possible long-term solutions to the party's electoral death spiral.

Faced with this new electoral reality, leaders will reportedly look at the potential policy consequences of the party's losses, reconsidering whether to push on with much-needed reforms to the healthcare and retirement systems, for instance.

Party leaders will also grapple with the fundamental question of how to deal with the AfD in the long run, namely, whether to maintain the party's "firewall" policy rejecting any cooperation or to work with the anti-immigrant rightwing populists in hopes of remaining relevant.

Speaking with Germany's Welt am Sonntag newspaper ahead of the pow-wow, Hesse State Premier Boris Rhein said leadership, "has to deal with all of the issues that are important to everyday citizens: Cost of living, security, immigration and jobs."

Skip next section This blog is on pause

This blog is on pause

We are pausing our coverage for now. Join us again on Sunday morning for more coverage of the German news and analysis.

Skip next section Germany rejects proposed EU budget, calls for greater cuts

Germany rejects proposed EU budget, calls for greater cuts

Germany swiftly rejected a proposed new budget for the European Union that was put forward on Saturday.

Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency, put forward a budget of €1.826 trillion ($2.046 trillion) for the next seven years — a reduction of around €159 billion compared to the European Commission's original proposal of nearly €1.985 trillion.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the budget cuts should go further.

"The size of the new proposal is no basis for an agreement," Merz said.

"The EU ​budget must be affordable for ⁠those who bear the main burden of financing," he added.

Germany is the largest net contributor to the EU budget. It and other net contributors including the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Austria and Finland all want the next budget to be slashed by hundreds of billions of euros.

But the second-largest net contributor to the EU budget, France, has instead argued that the 27-member bloc needs a more generous budget in order to overcome new challenges.

Skip next section 'Ragebait' named Germany's 2026 Youth Word of the Year

'Ragebait' named Germany's 2026 Youth Word of the Year

The Langenscheidt publishing house on Saturday named "ragebait" as Germany's 2026 Youth Word of the Year during the Frankfurt Book Fair.

Ragebait is social media content designed to draw people in by making them angry with provocative claims, lies, or outrageous opinions, thereby driving up clicks and interactions.

Langenscheidt, Germany's best-selling dictionary publisher, organized an online poll with 1 million young people taking part in this year's competition.

Ragebait took 36.5% of the vote, with runners-up including the terms "peak," meaning the best of the best, and "crashout," meaning when someone loses their cool.

Skip next section Germany 'committed' to further Russia sanctions

Germany 'committed' to further Russia sanctions

Germany on Saturday said it would continue pursuing sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine, coming a day after US President Donald Trump announced a temporary US sanctions reprieve on Russian diesel.

"The federal ⁠government ⁠has taken note of the US decision relating to Russian diesel deliveries," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement.

"The federal government ​remains committed to the decisions on ​sanctions against ‌Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," the statement added.

Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing ... Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue," he added.

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has been subject to round after round of sanctions packages led by the US and EU. 

Russian crude and other oil products have been subject to EU sanctions since 2023, and Germany has not imported any oil or oil products from Russia since then.

A spokesperson for Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche said Saturday that "Germany stands fully behind the sanctions packages."

"Our supply is diversified in this area; we are independent of Russian oil," the spokesperson said. 

Germany remains Ukraine's largest financial backer in Europe. During a visit to Kyiv last weekend, Chancellor Friedrich Merz reiterated Germany's unwavering support for Ukraine.

In what amounts to a major reversal in US policy, Trump on Friday said he would temporarily lift US sanctions to allow Russia to "immediately" supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.

The move comes as diesel prices reach record levels after the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel sent diesel prices skyrocketing around the world. In the US, the high prices are putting political pressure on Trump's Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November.

However, despite Trump's claims on social media, it remains unclear how much Russian fuel will reach global markets amid domestic fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to target refineries.

Skip next section Ex-Chancellor Schröder criticized for Putin birthday visit

Ex-Chancellor Schröder criticized for Putin birthday visit

The appearance of Germany's Russia-friendly former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder at President Vladimir Putin's birthday party earlier this week has drawn criticism in Germany.

Franziska Brantner, the co-leader of Germany's Green party, called on Schröder's Social Democrats (SPD) to revisit revoking Schröder's party membership.

"Russia is now even attacking us in Germany with hybrid attacks. Schröder hasn't learned anything from this. A new approach needs to be put on the table," she told the Tagesspiegel newspaper.

"Schröder is celebrating Putin's birthday with him, while civilians in Ukraine are once again dying as a result of Russian attacks. This is politically unacceptable," said Brantner.

Anything less than expulsion from the party would be "a disastrous signal, not only to Ukraine but also to the people and their safety in our country," Brantner added.

The SPD's Hubertus Heil, who served as Germany's labor minister from 2018 to 2025, also criticized Schröder.

"The warm embrace between Schröder and Putin in Moscow deeply outrages and disturbs me," Heil told the Tagesspiegel.

Celebrating with a "dictator" whose "murderous imperialism causes horrific suffering every day" is "unjustifiable under any circumstances," he said.

Putin celebrated his 74th birthday in Moscow on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Putin learned that Schröder was on a business trip in the Russian capital via Russian media reports. 

"The president invited his old friend to his home," the Kremlin said, with the Russian government releasing pictures of Schröder and Putin smiling and clasping hands,

Schröder's business and personal ties to Russia have drawn controversy since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Schröder's tax-payer financed Berlin office was closed in 2022 over his involvement in the Russian energy sector, but he fended off calls at the time by fellow party members to be expelled from the SPD.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from Bonn.

The German government said European sanctions on Russia will continune unabated after the Trump administration paused US sanctions on Russian diesel yesterday.

And Germany's former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder is under fire after attending Vladimir Putin's birthday in Moscow.

Read on for this and more.

entries.title: Couples looking to have children often turn to surrogacy agencies in Georgia without understanding the hidden costs
entries.summary: Georgia became a hub for surrogate pregnancies after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. DW spoke with parents, and those who wanted to become parents, about the hidden costs of a booming industry.
entries.content:
Europe

Surrogacy in Georgia is booming, but at what cost?

October 11, 2026

Georgia became a hub for surrogate pregnancies after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. DW spoke with parents, and those who wanted to become parents, about the hidden costs of a booming industry.

Three years ago, Olga, 40, and Daniel (both names changed to protect the their identities) from Hamburg decided to employ the services of a surrogate mother. But surrogacy is illegal in Germany, and people whose children are born through surrogacy must pursue the legal recognition of their parenthood in German courts.

Olga is a German citizen, but was born and raised in Russia. That's why the couple wanted to learn more about the surrogacy market in Russia. But foreign customers have been banned from signing Russian surrogacy contracts since 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, many international agencies that liaise between surrogates and intended parents moved to Georgia. So, Olga and Daniel traveled there.

Georgia the new destination for surrogate mothers

In the past years, Georgia, a mountainous country in the Caucasus region, has become a sort of surrogacy hub, with women traveling from all over the world to work as surrogates. According to Georgia's Public Service Development Agency, over 3,000 surrogate mothers were registered in 2023 across the country. Since 2012, they've given birth to over 5,000 children. And since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine, the number of children born to surrogate mothers has skyrocketed. While an estimated 300 surrogate mothers gave birth in 2021, that number leapt to over 1,100 by 2023.

Anastasia, 39, is a surrogate mother from Russia working in Georgia. She has a grown daughter and has already seen through three surrogate pregnancies. Her first was in 2021, which she used to finance a property down payment.

Anastasia says she completed her first two surrogacies in Russia, and her third — for a Japanese couple, brokered through the branch office of a Moscow clinic — in Georgia. Like many surrogate mothers, she went home to Russia after the embryo was implanted, and returned to Georgia when she was 22 weeks pregnant.

"I live in an apartment with another surrogate mother who carried twins to term. This program was the easiest and most practical one for me, but maybe I just got lucky with the right clinic," Anastasia told DW. "Other women who gave birth in Georgia told me they had difficulties. For example, after giving birth, they had to wait a long time before they were paid." She says she's ready to become a surrogate mother again.

Estimates vary, but there are about 19 clinics that offer such services across Georgia. And at around €45,000 ($50,400) to €55,000, the average service costs for agencies in Tbilisi or Batumi are only about a third of what agencies in other countries charge.

Several surrogate mothers who gave birth in Georgian clinics told DW that their average salary was between €18,000 and €28,000, with premiums added for birthing twins, for example.

Surrogate mothers from Ukraine in demand

Daniel and Olga told DW that they spent months looking for surrogacy agency in Georgia. "Pretty soon, we had access to a list of women from Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Georgia, and were given a detailed description of the process, along with the contact information of lawyers who could help take care of the formalities," they recount. "We were a little concerned that not every agency could give clear answers about the health of some of the surrogate mothers."

Both work in the medical field, and Olga says perhaps some of their questions about the physical health and possible genetic disorders might have been too probing. "We picked a 30-year-old woman from Ukraine who had already been a surrogate mother once for a European couple," she says. The Russian-Georgian agency set up half-hour long Zoom call, "but that hardly seemed enough to make a final decision," Olga adds.

In the spring of 2024, the married couple traveled to Georgia's capital to meet Elena (her name has been changed to protect her identity). Following a long discussion, the agency had seemed reluctant when they agreed to bring her to Tbilisi for the meeting. Elena made a good first impression on the couple from Hamburg, showing them pictures of her children and telling them she wanted to use the money she earned to renovate her apartment.

"They had initially told us that the surrogate would spent the entire pregnancy living in a rented apartment in Tbilisi," Olga and Daniel tell DW. "But then we found out that Elena was going back home for a few months after the embryo was implanted, back to Ukraine, where there's war."

Human rights experts criticize legislation

Georgian laws have a weak spot, the human rights lawyer Nino Bogveradze tells DW: They only regulate the relationship between the surrogate mothers, the intended parents, and the clinics, but they do not consider the roles that agencies play.

In Georgia, surrogate mothers have limited rights. Most concerns related to their pregnancy, medical care or payment are not regulated by national law but in contracts between the involved parties. And the state does not set minimum standards for social guarantees or contractual terms.

After an embryo has been implanted, surrogate mothers are not allowed to keep the child, leave the program, or end the pregnancy. Several human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the International Women's Health Coalition say the established practice in Georgia violates women's rights to reproductive self-determination.

Agencies guided by material interests

"Agencies often speak of their special mission to help people have the child they've been dreaming of," Olga Doletskaya from the University of Leeds tell DW. "But in reality, they're primarily driven by financial interests. And that's why they exploit the precarious situation of surrogate mothers, and pressure intended parents."

Olga and Daniel from Hamburg agree. "We were constantly being made to understand that we should decide as quickly as possible. We had to hurry because apparently several other couples were also interested in our surrogate," Olga says.

And the agency kept stressing that it had paid out of pocket for bringing the potential surrogate mother to Georgia, despite that not being contractually agreed. "At some point, a representative noticed my emotional state and asked me how long I wanted to remain childless," Olga recounts. "I felt like I was being manipulated."

The couple returned to Germany with mixed feelings and decided to shelve the idea of employing a surrogate mother — at least, for now.

Mark Sheider and Asja Lokina contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Russian.

entries.title: Demographic change: Germany's population is declining, but not everywhere
entries.summary: By 2045, Germany will have more older people, fewer workers, and a smaller population overall. Yet some regions will defy this trend. Their success depends on how much they have to offer.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany's population is shrinking, but not everywhere

October 11, 2026

By 2045, Germany will have more older people, fewer workers, and a smaller population overall. Yet some regions will defy this trend. Their success depends on how much they have to offer.

Germany's population is expected to decline from 83.5 million in 2025 to around 81.8 million by 2045, according to a new study from the Berlin Institute for Population and Development (Berlin-Institut für Bevölkerung und Entwicklung), in collaboration with the Wüstenrot Foundation, a non-profit that supports research on housing, urban development, and social change.

The decline in population alone is not the central challenge. More significant is the continuing rise in the number of retirees alongside a steadily shrinking workforce. Across Germany, the working-age population is projected to decrease by 4.7% by 2045.

"The baby boomer generation is retiring, while significantly smaller cohorts are following. Birth rates are falling, and immigration is not sufficient to offset the growing surplus of deaths over births," said Institute President Catherina Hinz when presenting the study in Berlin.

The term "baby boomers" refers to those born in the 1960s, when annual births exceeded one million. Thereafter, the birth rate fell sharply, effectively halving.

The economy matters

Germany's population may be shrinking, but according to the study, this trend is far from uniform across the country. In the years ahead, a region's economic attractiveness, and the financial strength that comes with it, will become even more important than it is today.

"Some regions will lose substantial numbers of residents and workers in the years ahead, while others continue to grow. Even within eastern Germany, southern Germany, and rural areas, the demographic and economic divide is widening," said Hinz.

"Demographic change is unfolding before our very eyes, and its effects are being felt across the country," Hinz added. "Its consequences can still be mitigated, but they can no longer be avoided. And the longer we wait, the narrower our scope for action will become."

Hinz's warning is echoed by Frederick Sixtus of the Berlin Institute. Almost every region now records more deaths than births, he notes, a consequence of decades of low birth rates. The implication is clear: Migration, both inward and outward, now shapes a region's demographic trajectory. Over recent decades, immigration from abroad has repeatedly helped stabilize population trends. Yet migration alone is no longer enough to halt the aging of society.

According to the study, several factors are critical if a region is to remain attractive to people relocating from abroad or from other parts of Germany: High-quality jobs offering good pay and working conditions, a sufficient supply of skilled workers for local businesses, financially robust municipalities, reliable childcare, and efficient transport and mobility infrastructure.

Berlin leads the way

Many major cities are expected to continue to grow in the years ahead, according to Manuel Slupina of the Wüstenrot Foundation. The study projects that Berlin will lead the way, with the capital's population increasing by almost 10% by 2045. Other cities expected to attract people include Hamburg, Frankfurt am Main, Munich, and Düsseldorf in western Germany, as well as Leipzig, Dresden, and Potsdam in the east.

The study's authors argue that the familiar distinction between urban and rural areas does not hold true everywhere. The hinterlands of many major cities are also expected to grow. While young people are increasingly drawn to metropolitan centers, families with children tend to settle in the surrounding areas. Among the places likely to lose population are several large cities in western Germany, including Bremen, Duisburg, Dortmund, and Kaiserslautern, whose economic appeal has gradually diminished. At the bottom of the ranking are many sparsely populated regions, a large number of them in eastern Germany.

Competition for talent

Twelve of the 20 districts and independent cities with the weakest overall ratings are now located in eastern Germany, up from five in the previous assessment in 2019. According to the study, these regions are also expected to see the steepest declines in their working-age populations, with losses of up to 18% by 2045. The authors conclude that competition for workers is therefore set to become one of the key demographic challenges of the decades ahead.

In this competition, the southern German states of Bavariaand Baden-Württemberg are regarded as having the strongest prospects. Bavaria ranks particularly highly thanks to its robust economy, which is thriving across much of the state, and its strong labor market. Women, older people, and people without German citizenship are also more likely to be employed in Bavaria than elsewhere. The ranking shows that economically successful regions are more effective at integrating different population groups into the labor market than weaker ones.

Policymakers must find local solutions

Under Germany's constitution, the country is committed to ensuring that people enjoy comparable opportunities, and with them the prospect of a good life, regardless of where they live.

The researchers offer clear recommendations to policymakers. They argue that the focus must be on addressing structural challenges and regional disparities. "What may be the right response for a growing major city is not necessarily the right one for a shrinking rural district," says Slupina. Tailor-made solutions are needed, but they require the right framework conditions. "There needs to be less rigid regulation, more scope for local initiative, and greater financial resources, especially for municipalities and those actively engaged at the local level." Slupina's message is clear: Regions should be trusted to shape their own futures.

Local authorities would no doubt welcome that. For years, mayors and district administrators have been calling for greater financial autonomy. They are currently seeking a larger share of overall tax revenues for municipalities. The federal government and the states, however, argue that they face budgetary constraints of their own. Yet both sides recognize that, sooner or later, Germany will have little choice but to reform its system of fiscal federalism.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Ukrainian prisoners of war and defectors have been gathered into a Russian battalion to face Ukrainian forces — why? And how?
entries.summary: Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian "volunteers." But veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Who are the Ukrainian 'volunteers' under Russian command?

October 11, 2026

Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian "volunteers." But veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts.

Pavlo Oliynyk, 25, says he joined enemy forces to escape Russian captivity. Before his capture in the Donbas region in 2024, he was a senior lieutenant for Ukraine's armed forces.

As a prisoner of war (POW), he says he was electrocuted, beaten, and psychologically tortured. So when he received the offer to join the Maksym Kryvonis battalion — named after a famous 17th-century Cossack commander — he accepted.

Oliynyk says he wanted to use this opportunity to reach the front lines, so he could escape to Ukrainian-controlled territory. DW was able to contact Oliynyk through his lawyer.

'Ukrainian volunteers' consist mostly of POWs

Reports of Russian combat units consisting of Ukrainian prisoners of war and former servicemembers of Ukraine's armed forces began emerging in late 2022. Several detachments were initially formed and in August 2026, they were merged into the so-called "Ukrainian Volunteer Special Forces Brigade."

Of the individual units, the Maksym Kryvonis battalion has perhaps drawn the most public attention for having evidently taken part in combat. Its true size is unknown — Russian media reports claim about 200 fighters while available footage only suggests several dozen.

An investigative team of the Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne has identified over 30 members and confirmed they are all former Ukrainian servicemen, captured by Russian forces between 2023 and 2024.

An 'imitation' of Russian legions fighting for Ukraine

Pavel Luzin, an expert for Russian foreign policy and defense at the Center for European Policy Analysis, believes these units are an "imitation" of the Russian Volunteer Corps and the Freedom of Russia Legion — units in the Ukrainian armed forces, consisting of Russian citizens — and an attempt by Moscow to distract from the fact that these units exist in the first place. Ukrainian intelligence services tend to agree.

"It bothers them that Russians would fight on Ukraine's side, but Ukrainians won't fight on Russia's side," Yevhen Shybalov, author and veteran of the war in Ukraine, tells DW. He adds that Russian troops have never tried to hide the fact that Russian volunteer units in Ukrainian ranks were the main reason Russian forces wanted to create Ukrainian units for their owns ranks.

Just how voluntary are these combat units?

In 2025, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) reported that 95% of the released Ukrainian POWs interviewed reported torture or ill-treatment during Russian captivity.

Bill Wiley, executive director of the NGO Commission for International Justice and Accountability (CIJA), says that the physical and psychological state of the returned combatants raises serious doubts that their recruitment was voluntary. Mykhailo Savva of the Center for Civil Liberties, a Kyiv-based human rights organization, points to the criminal procedures running against several of the battalion members, which he says indicates that these suggest the combatants had switched sides voluntarily.

But where to draw the line between voluntary and involuntary recruitment? The war veteran and human rights activist Maksym Butkevych, who spent 28 months as a prisoner of war, says the conditions in Russian captivity make that line hard to distinguish. On the one hand, he says, there is a constant atmosphere of pressure, and on the other hand, it's not implausible that some prisoners defected out of ideological proximity.

How were Ukrainian prisoners made to join Russian forces?

Butkevych tells DW that between 2022 and 2023, all Ukrainian prisoners of war had received offers, "more or less persistently," to join the Russian army. In his case, he recounts, it was after he had been severely mistreated. "They showed us they could do anything they wanted to us," the veteran explains, "which was why we should agree to everything."

The veteran Shybalov reports similar experiences. He speaks of attempts to force confessions of war crimes, or to recruit members for Russia's intelligence services, and tells DW all prisoners were first interrogated and then made certain propositions under duress.

"You can torture people to get them to confess, but there comes the difficult moment when you need to give them a weapon," he says. "That's why it's more about psychological pressure, and forcing voluntary compliance."

Butkevych confirms these accounts with his own tales. But neither veteran has ever met someone willing to join Russian units, they say.

What happens after conscription?

Oliynyk, from the Maksym Kryvonis battalion, says he initially turned down multiple bids to join Russian forces. He says he only accepted the fourth offer so he could flee.

He claims he didn't sign official Defense Ministry paperwork, but a private contract with an individual offering military services. Afterwards, he says, he was brought to a room where he heard lectures and saw videos and photos he was later asked to retell.

Control and mistreatment

He says fellow servicemembers in the Maksym Kryvonis battalion consisted both of those who had switched sides of their own volition, and those who had been forced.

In a video circulating online that appears to be of a trial in Ukraine, he also says that former Ukrainian POWs in the unit were followed and guarded by mercenaries of the private military company Redut. In the same video, he also speaks of beatings and torture, and receiving monthly wages in envelopes handed out by a member of Russia's military intelligence.

He tells DW he had been given a phone, but that he was too scared to call anyone in Ukraine because it was under constant surveillance. He denies having fought against Ukrainians, as he fled in March 2025 before his first deployment in the Donetsk province. After running across a field, he says he spent two days hiding from drones in basements and houses before making contact with Ukrainian fighters.

Now, Oliynyk has been in detention in Ukraine for nearly two years while authorities investigate possible treason. He has yet to be formally charged.

Sergey Nikitin contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Ukrainian.

entries.title: India's 'Cockroach' movement leaders say 'the fight has just begun' after a large protest in Delhi
entries.summary: Leaders of the youth-led protest movement demanding India's election commissioner step down say the "fight has just begun" after they were released from detention following a large demonstration in Delhi. More on DW.
entries.content:
India

India: 'Cockroach' leaders vow new protests after release

Published October 11, 2026last updated October 11, 2026

Leaders of the youth-led protest movement demanding India's election commissioner step down say the "fight has just begun" after they were released from detention following a large demonstration in Delhi. More on DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here are the latest developments from India on Sunday, October 11:

  • The CJP said leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were ordered released after nearly 24 hours of detention
  • Indian media reports cite Delhi Police officials as saying thousands of detained protesters were released
  • The CJP called for a fresh protest on Sunday

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section How has the BJP reacted to the protests against India's election chief?

How has the BJP reacted to the protests against India's election chief?

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) says that protests over alleged voter list manipulation are an attempt to "create a highly dangerous and serious situation in the country." 

The party has denounced the CJP and the INDIA bloc of opposition parties as "anarchists".

"Right now, there's a race in the country to prove who is how big an anarchist," BJP National President Nitin Nabin said on Saturday, adding this included Rahul Gandhi's 'INDI alliance' and the leaders of the "Cockroach" movement

These sentiments were also echoed by BJP MP Bansuri Swaraj at press briefing on Sunday.

"It seems a competition in creating anarchy is emerging between Arvind Kejriwal and Rahul Gandhi. Whether it is the Aam Aadmi Party or the Congress, the country's revered voters have rejected both. Having failed to secure power through the people's mandate, they are now looking for excuses for their defeat," Swaraj told reporters.

CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke railed against Modi in a post on X, shortly after the activist leader was released from detention on Sunday.

"Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India," Dipke said, while calling the Indian leader as a "coward" and "bully."

Modi was in Tamil Nadu's capital Chennai on Sunday for a series of engagements, including laying foundation stones for development projects estimated to be worth over 130 billion Indian rupees. He has yet to directly address the latest CJP protests this weekend.

Skip next section CJP issues fresh appeal for peaceful protests

CJP issues fresh appeal for peaceful protests

CJP co-convenor Saurav Das called on people from across India to again protest in a peaceful manner.

"This demonstration is still on," Das said as he spoke about reported protester detentions taking place for a second day.

"We are not going to move back, we appeal to all Indian citizens that you will have to fight. You will have to come out on the streets. Wherever you are, you will have to do a peaceful demonstration," he told a press conference.

"This system cannot go on like this. This system is broken. This system is corrupt… and this system only works in the service of two people," Das said, going on to name Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah.

The CJP's Ashutosh Ranka said peaceful protesters who wanted to demonstrate at a designated protest site were picked up.

"The fight has just begun…Modi and Shah should feel ashamed for treating this fight like a war," he said.

Skip next section CJP leaders hold press conference after release from preventive detention

CJP leaders hold press conference after release from preventive detention

"Cockroach" protest movement leader Saurav Das told reporters at a press conference in New Delhi that Prime Minister Narendra Modi is putting India in a "civil war-like situation,"

Das spoke to reporters hours after he was released from detention along with co-leaders Abhijeet Dipke and Ashutosh Ranka.

Ranka and CJP legal head Ratna Singh were also present at the press conference.

Das accused the police of "arriving like mafia dons" and "abducting" them on Saturday when they were detained from a plane upon landing in New Delhi.

He alleged they were not allowed to meet their lawyers while in detention.

Skip next section New protest arrests reported in Delhi

New protest arrests reported in Delhi

More detentions are being reported in New Delhi as India's election protest appears to be entering a second day.

Several protesters were seen marching towards the protest site in Jantar Mantar in images circulating on Indian media.

News agency ANI reported that some people were detained at the inner circle of Connaught Place, close to Jantar Mantar, where student and youth organizations of opposition parties were protesting.

Meanwhile, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which is organizing protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, shared a series of videos on X, alleging fresh detentions.

"Detain us, arrest us, do whatever you can! We will not be intimidated. This is just the beginning. We will continue fighting until all our demands are met," the CJP’s Ajinkya Shinde said on X.

Skip next section India slams UN human rights body's statement on detentions

India slams UN human rights body's statement on detentions

India on Sunday rejected remarks by the United Nations Office for the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) that called on Indian authorities to immediately release "arbitrarily detained" people during Saturday's protest. 

"We are concerned by reports of mass detentions in India of demonstrators, protest leaders, members of civil society organisations, lawyers and journalists, before and during today's large-scale demonstrations in Delhi," the OHCHR said in a statement on Saturday.

"All those arbitrarily detained must be immediately and unconditionally released."

India's Foreign Ministry called the UN office's concerns "unwarranted" and said that they "constitute an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs" of the country.

"India is the world's largest democracy, where the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by our Constitution and safeguarded by robust institutions, an independent judiciary and a free media," the ministry said in a statement on Sunday.

"As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to the maintenance of public order and safety. Our law enforcement authorities act strictly in accordance with the law, and our courts remain available to all for the redressal of any grievances."

The ministry went on to accuse the UN human rights agency of having an "approach of extreme selectivity" on public positions.

The ministry said it had noted that "violent responses to protests" in India's neighborhood have gone "uncommented, as indeed have law enforcement actions in its own vicinity."

The statement accused the OHCHR of "double standards" which it continued to say "only erode the credibility" of the body and "contribute to the loss of faith in multilateralism."

Skip next section What is the latest on the protests?

What is the latest on the protests?

The CJP is set to hold a press conference in New Delhi at 2 p.m. local time (8.30 am UTC) today, the group said Sunday.

Meanwhile, it is yet to be seen if a fresh protest in New Delhi will take place. On Saturday evening, temporary protest leader Ajinkya Shinde had called for new demonstrations.

Earlier on X, Shinde said that a protest was scheduled in Mumbai at 4 p.m. adding that more cities "will follow."

As of early afternoon in Delhi, there were no signs of any major gathering of protesters around the Jantar Mantar site in the center of the city.



On Saturday, Mumbai too saw a series of detentions at a protest against the chief election commissioner over alleged electoral roll irregularities.

According to reports, around 600 protesters were detained and later released. The detainees included Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of India's independence icon Mahatma Gandhi, and Bollywood actor Imran Khan.

Skip next section Why do protesters want election chief Gyanesh Kumar to resign?

Why do protesters want election chief Gyanesh Kumar to resign?

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) started as an online satirical movement and sprung to the mainstream as a pressure group in July after forcing the resignation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's then education minister amid massive youth-led demonstrations.

Now the CJP movement has Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in its crosshairs.

Here is a ten-point breakdown of the controversy surrounding the top election official:

  • The protests concern a contentious, nationwide voter-verification exercise — called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — which began last year. Around 130 million names have been removed so far from electoral rolls under the process.
  • Kumar heads the three-member Election Commission of India (ECI) overseeing the SIR process.
  • Last Month, The Indian Express newspaper published a report alleging differences within the ECI over decisions related to the SIR.
  • According to The Indian Express, Kumar's two fellow election commissioners raised at least 14 formal objections over a 10-month period regarding voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral roll data, but their concerns were allegedly not taken into consideration.
  • The report said that in one objection, one of the commissioners complained that the ECI had acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."
  • The report sparked a political storm with protests calling for Kumar's resignation, allegedly for undermining the poll body's credibility.
  • The ECI has maintained that all its decisions were lawful, saying that differing views were a routine part of the decision-making process.
  • Kumar is yet to address the allegations against him.
  • Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large number of minority voters.
  • They accuse Modi's BJP party of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains and question the ECI's independence. The ECI says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and helps prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

The CJP is not the only group calling for Kumar's resignation.

India's bloc of opposition parties, led by Congress' Rahul Gandhi, has been carrying out a sustained campaign against Kumar in recent days, including organizing its own protest marches.

Skip next section 'Cockroach ' leaders released on condition of 'no breach of peace' for a year — reports

'Cockroach ' leaders released on condition of 'no breach of peace' for a year — reports

Cockroach Janta Party leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were released from detention on condition that they made "no breach of peace for one year," according to reports citing the movement's legal head, Ratna Singh, on Sunday. 

In a post on X cited by the AFP news agency, Singh said the three had been released on the condition that they make "no breach of peace for one year."

News agency ANI reported the Delhi Police as saying the movement's leaders were placed under "preventive arrest" on Saturday, and that a bail bond of 50,000 rupees (€ 460) was filled for "maintaining peace and good behavior for a period of one year."

Skip next section YouTuber Dhurv Rathee released from detention

YouTuber Dhurv Rathee released from detention

Social media influencer Dhruv Rathee, who was detained from his Gurugram residence on Saturday morning ahead protests in Delhi, was released overnight, reports said.

Reuters news agency cited an anonymous Interior Ministry official as saying that Rathee was released on condition that he would not take part in any further protests.

On Friday night, Rathee had uploaded a video of himself standing in front of New Delhi's iconic India Gate, where he called out the elaborate restrictions authorities had put in place to counter the protests planned by the Cockroach movement.

Skip next section Supreme Court holds special Sunday hearing on protest curbs, detentions

Supreme Court holds special Sunday hearing on protest curbs, detentions

A rare Sunday hearing is set to take place in India's top court over a contempt petition against a set of transportation restrictions during a large-scale protest in New Delhi a day earlier. 

The petition accuses authorities of closing metro stations despite a Supreme Court order against a complete shutdown of public transport ahead of the protest.

On Friday, authorities had ordered the closure of more than 50 metro stations and canceled many trains bound for two major railway stations in the capital in a bid to keep protesters from heading to central Delhi.

But the Supreme Court later directed the government to not completely stop train services and said that there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.

The court was also scheduled to hear petitions challenging the detentions of thousands of protesters, Cockroach Janta Party leaders and political leaders from India's opposition parties.

Skip next section 'Cockroach' leaders ordered released from detention, party says

'Cockroach' leaders ordered released from detention, party says

An executive court in Delhi has ordered the release of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder  Abhijeet Dipke and other leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, the youth-led movement said on Sunday.

The three were detained ahead of a large protest in Dehli on Saturday and appeared in court earlier on Sunday after being in detention for nearly 24 hours.

Earlier, the CJP had alleged the leaders were being detained at an undisclosed location and did not have access to their lawyers.

On Saturday evening, the CJP issued a fresh call for a march to New Delhi's Jantar Mantar on Sunday.

"We're not backing down! We will march to Jantar Mantar again tomorrow," Ajinkya Shinde, the CJP's interim protest leader, said at a press conference.

The exact number of demonstrators detained during the protest could not be immediately verified.

Shinde told reporters that over 15,000 people, including students, had been detained across India.

The Hindu newspaper, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that 2,500 demonstrators were detained in Delhi on top of 1,000 people picked up in overnight preventive measures ahead of the protest.

Indian media reports cite Delhi Police as saying that all detainees had been released later on Saturday.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's Studio in New Delhi, bringing you the Sunday edition of the India news blog.

We are continuing our coverage of the intensifying election protests in India over alleged manipulation of voter lists.

Here's a quick recap of what went down on Saturday:

Dramatic scenes unfolded in the streets of the capital of the world's largest democracy on Saturday as authorities tried to thwart a protest called by the "Cockroach" movement calling for the resignation of India's election chief.

Thousands of youth protesters were detained and hauled away in buses as parts of Delhi were locked down with a mammoth deployment of police and paramilitary personnel, who essentially outnumbered the demonstrators.

Mobile internet services were suspended in central Delhi in a rare move for the key power district, while dozens of metro stations were closed.

Police cited violation of a ban on the protest as basis for the mass detentions. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and student organizations supporting the demonstration maintain that they did not need permission, citing protesting as a fundamental right. 

The three main faces of the CJP — Founder Abhijeet Dipke, Co-conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka — were detained onboard a plane as soon as they landed in New Delhi for the protest.

Meanwhile, four former chief ministers of Indian states were also briefly detained during the protest, amid the opposition parties stepping up their calls for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Stay tuned as we bring you more.
